new_statements.quote: There are nineteen phonemes in Upper Tanudan Kalinga: fourteen consonants and five vowels. The consonants are /p,t,b,d,g,m,n,ng,s,l,w,y/ and glottal stops /k/ and /-/. The vowels are /i,u,o,e,a/. Word stress and consonant length are also phonemic. There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC. [1991:190] — 1985:124 reads: 'Stress and consonant length are also phonemic. There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC.'

There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC.' (the text renders the slashes as I/l, which the compiler normalised; the stress sentence is character-for-character identical). new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is a lexically contrastive (phonemic) property of the word, on a par with consonant gemination; the author gives no rule for where it falls, so placement is treated as unpredictable from the source's standpoint (typical Central Cordilleran penult/final contrast is not stated here).
new_statements.exceptions: None. No placement rule, no examples of minimal pairs, no orthographic marking; the only other datum is the SIL 2012 Lower Tanudan [kml] orthography fact sheet: 'Stress is phonemic, but is marked only in the dictionary.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Word stress'); described from the Lubo village dialect ('Linurubu'), Tanudan Valley, fieldwork 1982-1985 under SIL. Neither the 1985 texts nor the 1991 examples mark stress, so no positional data can be recovered from the corpus.
new_statements.identity_note: ISO 639-3 [kgh] Upper Tanudan Kalinga was retired by CR 2011-079 (2012-02-03) and merged into [kml] Lower Tanudan Kalinga, renamed 'Tanudan Kalinga' (rationale: no basic communication difference between Upper and Lower Tanudan); Glottolog keeps uppe1424 as a Bookkeeping languoid, the living entry being lowe1412 'Tanudan Kalinga' (kml). Brainard's description is of the Lubo village dialect ('Linurubu'; villages Lubo, Gaang, Dacalan, ~3,000 speakers in 1985), which Himes 1997 (OL 36:102-134) groups with Mangali as Southeastern Kalinga (KLASE). Any lowe1412 catalog entry built on Minangali/Lower Tanudan sources (Olson et al. 2008; SIL 2012 fact sheet: 'Stress is phonemic, but is marked only in the dictionary') describes the other dialect of the same ISO language; the two should count as one entity for the census, with the Brainard statement filed as the Lubo-dialect statement.

sources.note: Appendix B 'Phonology', 1. General sketch, p.190: 'Word stress and consonant length are also phonemic.' Nothing on placement, secondary stress, or marking; texts carry no stress marks.

Only a Lubuagan Kalinga orthography note (after Hohulin & Zamora 1995): acute accent may mark stress to distinguish chílu 'honey' vs chilú 'dew'; lists Tanudan Kalinga dialects Minangali, Tinaloctoc, Pinangol, Dacalan, Lubo. Not a Tanudan statement.
